Phở là một món ăn truyền thống của Việt Nam, được xem là một trong những món ăn tiêu biểu cho nền ẩm thực Việt Nam.
Thành phần chính của phở là bánh phở và nước dùng cùng với thịt bò hoặc thịt gà cắt lát mỏng, hành.
Nước dùng của phở bò thường được ninh từ xương ống bò kèm với các loại gia vị như quế, hồi, thảo quả nướng.
Một trong những tài liệu đầu tiên nhắc đến phở là cuốn từ điển Hán-Việt Nhật Dụng Thường Đàm của Phạm Đình Hổ biên soạn vào năm 1827.
Phở như ngày nay được cho là đã ra đời và định hình vào những năm đầu thế kỷ 20, với Hà Nội và Nam Định thường được cho là hai địa phương xuất xứ của phở.
Danh từ 'phở' được chính thức ấn hành lần đầu trong cuốn Việt Nam tự điển (1930) do Hội Khai Trí Tiến Đức khởi thảo, với định nghĩa 'Món đồ ăn bằng bánh thái nhỏ nấu với thịt bò'.
Năm 1939, phở gà xuất hiện vì mỗi tuần có hai ngày (thứ hai và thứ sáu) không có thịt bò bán do việc giết mổ trâu bò bị hạn chế, khiến nhiều chủ quán phở bò phải đóng cửa vào những ngày đó.
Phở là món ăn tổ hợp của các chất vị; trong bát phở có chứa 18-20 loại thực phẩm gốc động vật và thực vật tự nhiên.
Phở bắt nguồn từ Bắc Bộ, xâm nhập vào Trung Bộ giữa thập niên 1950, sau sự thất bại của Pháp ở Đông Dương và Việt Nam bị chia thành 2 miền.
Phở Sài Gòn (phở Nam) thường đi kèm với các gia vị tương đen, tương ớt, chanh, rau sống (ngò gai, húng quế) và giá, trong khi tại Hà Nội thông thường sẽ không có đĩa rau sống này.
Năm 2016, người Nhật đã chọn ngày 4 tháng 4 hàng năm là Ngày phở Việt Nam tại Nhật Bản, vì số 4 (four) trong tiếng Anh và từ 'phở' đều phiên âm bằng tiếng Nhật là フォー (fō), giúp mọi người dễ nhớ.
Vào tháng 8/2024, phở Hà Nội, phở Nam Định và mì Quảng được Bộ Văn hóa Thể thao và Du lịch công nhận là Di sản văn hóa phi vật thể quốc gia.
Random forests or random decision forests is an ensemble learning method for classification, regression, and other tasks that works by creating a multitude of decision trees during training.
For classification tasks, the output of the random forest is the class selected by most trees.
For regression tasks, the output of the random forest is the average of the predictions of the trees.
Random forests correct for decision trees' habit of overfitting to their training set.
The first algorithm for random decision forests was created in 1995 by Tin Kam Ho using the random subspace method.
Leo Breiman and Adele Cutler developed an extension of the algorithm that combines Breiman's 'bagging' idea with random selection of features, and registered 'Random Forests' as a trademark in 2006.

The general method of random decision forests was first proposed by Salzberg and Heath in 1993, using a randomized decision tree algorithm to create multiple trees that are then combined using majority voting.

Ho established that forests of trees splitting with oblique hyperplanes can gain accuracy as they grow without suffering from overtraining, as long as the forests are randomly restricted to be sensitive to only selected feature dimensions.

Breiman's paper describing random forests combines a CART-like procedure for building a forest of uncorrelated trees with randomized node optimization and bagging, and introduces using out-of-bag error as an estimate of generalization error and measuring variable importance through permutation.

According to Hastie et al., decision tree learning is close to an 'off-the-shelf procedure for data mining' because it is invariant under scaling and other transformations of feature values, is robust to inclusion of irrelevant features, and produces inspectable models -- but decision trees are seldom accurate.
Trees that are grown very deep tend to learn highly irregular patterns and overfit their training sets, meaning they have low bias but very high variance.

Random forests average multiple deep decision trees trained on different parts of the same training set to reduce variance, at the expense of a small increase in bias and some loss of interpretability.

The bagging training algorithm for random forests repeatedly, B times, samples with replacement n training examples from the training set to form a sample Xb, Yb, and trains a classification or regression tree on each sample.
After training, predictions for unseen samples are made by averaging the predictions of all the individual regression trees, or by taking the plurality vote in the case of classification trees.

The bootstrapping procedure leads to better model performance because it decreases the variance of the model without increasing the bias, so the average of many trees is not highly sensitive to noise in the training set as long as the trees are not correlated.

Simply training many trees on a single training set would give strongly correlated trees, or even the same tree many times if the training algorithm is deterministic; bootstrap sampling de-correlates the trees by showing them different training sets.

The number B of samples (equivalently, of trees) is a free parameter; typically a few hundred to several thousand trees are used, depending on the size and nature of the training set, and B can be optimized using cross-validation or by observing the out-of-bag error.

Random forests also use 'feature bagging' -- a modified tree learning algorithm that selects a random subset of the features at each candidate split -- because if one or a few features are very strong predictors, ordinary bootstrap samples would select those features in many of the B trees, causing the trees to become correlated.
For regression problems, the inventors recommend a default minimum node size of 5, though in practice the best values for such parameters should be tuned on a case-by-case basis for every problem.

Extremely randomized trees (ExtraTrees) are an ensemble of individual trees like ordinary random forests but differ in two main ways: each tree is trained using the whole learning sample rather than a bootstrap sample, and the top-down splitting is randomized by choosing a number of random cut-points per feature instead of computing the locally optimal cut-point.

In ExtraTrees, cut-point values for a feature are chosen from a uniform distribution within the feature's empirical range in the tree's training set, rather than computing the locally optimal cut-point (based on, e.g., information gain or Gini impurity); among all the randomly chosen splits, the split yielding the highest score is chosen to split the node.

The basic random forest procedure may not work well in situations where there are a large number of features but only a small proportion of these features are informative with respect to sample classification.

Methods for addressing random forests' difficulty with high-dimensional, mostly uninformative feature sets include prefiltering (eliminating features that are mostly just noise), Enriched Random Forest (using weighted random sampling that gives greater weight to more informative features), and Tree-weighted random forest (giving more weight to more accurate trees).

Permutation importance is computed by training a random forest and recording the out-of-bag error for each data point averaged over the forest, then permuting a feature's values in the out-of-bag samples, recomputing the out-of-bag error, and averaging the difference in error before and after the permutation over all trees, normalized by the standard deviation of the differences.

Permutation importance has drawbacks: when features have different numbers of values, random forests favor features with more values; if the data contain groups of correlated features of similar relevance, smaller groups are favored over large groups; and if there are collinear features, the procedure may fail to identify important features unless groups of correlated features are permuted together.

Mean decrease in impurity feature importance considers as important the variables which decrease a lot the impurity during splitting; it is described in Breiman's book Classification and Regression Trees and is the default implementation in scikit-learn and R, with normalized importance obtained so the sum of normalized feature importances across all features is 1.
Statistics commonly used as an impurity measure for samples falling in a node include entropy, the Gini coefficient, and mean squared error.

The scikit-learn default mean-decrease-in-impurity feature importance implementation can report misleading feature importance because it favors high cardinality features and uses training statistics, so it does not reflect a feature's usefulness for predictions on a test set.

A relationship between random forests and the k-nearest neighbor algorithm (k-NN) was pointed out by Lin and Jeon in 2002; both can be viewed as weighted neighborhoods schemes that make predictions for new points by looking at a weight function over the training set, and since a forest averages the predictions of a set of trees with individual weight functions, the whole forest is again a weighted neighborhood scheme.

Random forest predictors naturally lead to a dissimilarity measure among observations; this can be extended to define dissimilarity between unlabeled data by training a forest to distinguish original observed data from synthetic data drawn from a reference distribution, and this random forest dissimilarity has been used, for example, to find clusters of patients based on tissue marker data.

Instead of decision trees, linear models such as multinomial logistic regression and naive Bayes classifiers have been proposed and evaluated as base estimators in random forests; in cases where the relationship between the predictors and the target variable is linear, these base learners may have accuracy equal to that of the ensemble learner.

Kernel random forests (KeRF) establish a connection between random forests and kernel methods: by slightly modifying their definition, random forests can be rewritten as kernel methods, which are more interpretable and easier to analyze.

Centered forest and uniform forest are two simplified models of Breiman's original random forest: centered forest uniformly selects an attribute among all attributes and splits at the center of the cell along that attribute until a fully binary tree of a given level is built, while uniform forest uniformly selects a feature and splits at a point uniformly drawn on the side of the cell along that feature.

While random forests often achieve higher accuracy than a single decision tree, they sacrifice the intrinsic interpretability of decision trees, because following the path a single decision tree takes to make its decision is trivial, but following the paths of tens or hundreds of trees is much harder.

To achieve both performance and interpretability, some model compression techniques allow transforming a random forest into a minimal 'born-again' decision tree that faithfully reproduces the same decision function.

Another limitation of random forests is that if features are linearly correlated with the target, the random forest may not enhance the accuracy of the base learner, and likewise in problems with multiple categorical variables.
Gradient descent is a method for unconstrained mathematical optimization; it is a first-order iterative algorithm for minimizing a differentiable multivariate function.

The idea of gradient descent is to take repeated steps in the direction opposite to the gradient (or approximate gradient) of the function at the current point, because this is the direction of steepest descent.
Stepping in the direction of the gradient, rather than opposite to it, leads to a trajectory that maximizes the function; this procedure is known as gradient ascent.
Gradient descent should not be confused with local search algorithms, although both are iterative methods for optimization.
Gradient descent is particularly useful in machine learning and artificial intelligence for minimizing the cost or loss function.
Gradient descent is generally attributed to Augustin-Louis Cauchy, who first suggested it in 1847.
Jacques Hadamard independently proposed a similar method to gradient descent in 1907.
The convergence properties of gradient descent for non-linear optimization problems were first studied by Haskell Curry in 1944.
Stochastic gradient descent, a simple extension of gradient descent, serves as the most basic algorithm used for training most deep networks today.

Gradient descent is based on the observation that if a multi-variable function is defined and differentiable in a neighborhood of a point, then the function decreases fastest if one moves from that point in the direction of the negative gradient of the function at that point.

It is possible to guarantee convergence to a local minimum under certain assumptions on the function, such as convexity and Lipschitz continuity, combined with particular choices of step size, including a sequence as in the Barzilai-Borwein method or a sequence satisfying the Wolfe conditions found via line search.
When the function being minimized is convex, all local minima are also global minima, so in this case gradient descent can converge to the global solution.

The basic intuition behind gradient descent can be illustrated by a hypothetical scenario of people stuck on a foggy mountain who use the steepness of the hill at their current position, measured with a sophisticated instrument analogous to differentiation, to proceed in the direction of steepest descent, taking measurements at intervals analogous to the step size.

Using a step size that is too small would slow convergence, while a step size that is too large would lead to overshoot and divergence, making the choice of a good step size an important practical problem.

In choosing a step size and descent direction, the update direction should point downhill; the amount by which the function can be guaranteed to decrease depends on a trade-off between the angle of the descent direction relative to the negative gradient and how quickly the gradient changes along the descent direction.

One way to choose a step size is to set the descent direction to the negative gradient and use line search to find a suitable step size, such as one satisfying the Wolfe conditions; a more economical alternative with good theoretical guarantees and experimental results is backtracking line search.

subtopic: approaches to choosing step and direction
fact_text: Approaches for choosing the step size and descent direction include using the Hessian to estimate curvature (if the function is twice-differentiable), using the function's Lipschitz constant to bound curvature, or building a custom model of the function; under stronger assumptions such as convexity, more advanced techniques may be possible.

Gradient descent can be used to solve a system of linear equations by reformulating it as a quadratic minimization problem; if the system matrix is real symmetric and positive-definite, an objective function is defined as a quadratic function whose minimization is equivalent to solving the linear system.

For quadratic functions, the line search minimization that finds the locally optimal step size on every iteration can be performed analytically, and explicit formulas for the locally optimal step size are known.
Gradient descent (steepest descent) is rarely used for solving linear equations, with the conjugate gradient method being one of the most popular alternatives.

The number of gradient descent iterations needed is commonly proportional to the spectral condition number of the system matrix (the ratio of the maximum to minimum eigenvalues of the matrix), while the convergence of the conjugate gradient method is typically determined by a square root of the condition number, making it much faster; both methods can benefit from preconditioning, though gradient descent may require fewer assumptions on the preconditioner.

Because each steepest-descent step is taken in the steepest direction, the steps alternate between directions aligned with the extreme axes of elongated level sets; when the condition number of the system matrix is large, this produces a characteristic zig-zag path, and the poor conditioning of the matrix is the primary cause of the slow convergence.

Gradient descent can be used to solve a system of nonlinear equations; in a worked example with three unknown variables, x1, x2, and x3, a Jacobian matrix is computed at an initial guess and used to take one iteration step of gradient descent.

Gradient descent works in spaces of any number of dimensions, even infinite-dimensional ones; in the infinite-dimensional case, the search space is typically a function space, and the Frechet derivative of the functional to be minimized is calculated to determine the descent direction.

Gradient descent can take many iterations to compute a local minimum with a required accuracy if the curvature in different directions is very different for the given function; preconditioning, which changes the geometry of the space to shape the function's level sets like concentric circles, cures this slow convergence but can be computationally expensive to construct and apply.

Methods based on Newton's method and inversion of the Hessian using conjugate gradient techniques can be better alternatives to gradient descent, generally converging in fewer iterations though the cost of each iteration is higher; for extremely large problems where computer-memory issues dominate, a limited-memory method such as L-BFGS should be used instead of BFGS or steepest descent.

Although it is sometimes possible to substitute gradient descent for a local search algorithm, gradient descent is not in the same family: it is an iterative method for local optimization that relies on an objective function's gradient rather than an explicit exploration of a solution space.
Gradient descent can be viewed as applying Euler's method for solving ordinary differential equations to a gradient flow.

Gradient descent can converge to a local minimum and slow down in the neighborhood of a saddle point; even for unconstrained quadratic minimization, gradient descent develops a zig-zag pattern of subsequent iterates as iterations progress, resulting in slow convergence.

Yurii Nesterov proposed a modification that enables faster convergence for convex problems; for unconstrained smooth problems this is called the fast gradient method (FGM) or accelerated gradient method (AGM), and using the Nesterov acceleration technique reduces the error in the objective value compared to standard gradient descent, with the resulting decrease rate known to be optimal for first-order optimization methods.
The optimized gradient method (OGM) reduces the constant factor of the optimal first-order convergence rate by a factor of two and is an optimal first-order method for large-scale problems.

The momentum or heavy ball method, used to break the zig-zag pattern of gradient descent, uses a momentum term in analogy to a heavy ball sliding on the surface of the function's values; gradient descent with momentum remembers the solution update at each iteration and determines the next update as a linear combination of the gradient and the previous update.
For unconstrained quadratic minimization, the theoretical convergence rate bound of the heavy ball method is asymptotically the same as that for the optimal conjugate gradient method.

Gradient descent can be extended to handle constraints by including a projection onto the set of constraints, a method that is only feasible when the projection is efficiently computable on a computer and is a specific case of the forward-backward algorithm for monotone inclusions.
Gradient descent is a special case of mirror descent using the squared Euclidean distance as the given Bregman divergence.

If the objective function is assumed to be strongly convex and Lipschitz smooth, gradient descent converges linearly with a fixed step size; looser assumptions lead to either weaker convergence guarantees or require a more sophisticated step size selection.
Precision (also called positive predictive value) is the fraction of relevant instances among the retrieved instances.
Recall (also known as sensitivity) is the fraction of relevant instances that were retrieved.

In a picture containing ten cats and twelve dogs, a program that identifies eight dogs (of which five are actually dogs) has precision 5/8 (true positives / selected elements) and recall 5/12 (true positives / relevant elements); the three misidentified cats are false positives and the seven missed dogs are false negatives.

In hypothesis-testing terms, absence of Type I and Type II errors (perfect specificity and sensitivity) corresponds respectively to perfect precision (no false positives) and perfect recall (no false negatives); recall is simply the complement of the Type II error rate (one minus the Type II error rate).

Precision can be seen as a measure of quality, and recall as a measure of quantity: higher precision means an algorithm returns more relevant results than irrelevant ones, while high recall means it returns most of the relevant results (whether or not irrelevant ones are also returned).

In a classification task, precision for a class is the number of true positives divided by the total number of elements labelled as belonging to the positive class (true positives plus false positives); recall is the number of true positives divided by the total number of elements that actually belong to the positive class (true positives plus false negatives).

Precision and recall are not particularly useful when used in isolation: it is possible to have perfect recall by simply retrieving every item, and it is possible to achieve perfect precision by selecting only a very small number of extremely likely items.

A smoke detector is generally designed to commit many Type I errors (alerting when there is no danger) because the cost of a Type II error (failing to sound an alarm during a major fire) is prohibitively high, so smoke detectors are designed favoring recall over precision.

Blackstone's ratio, "It is better that ten guilty persons escape than that one innocent suffer," emphasizes the cost of a Type I error (convicting an innocent person); accordingly the criminal justice system is geared toward precision, even at the cost of losses in recall (letting more guilty people go free).

A brain surgeon removing a tumor illustrates the tradeoff: being more liberal in the brain tissue removed increases recall (more cancer cells extracted) but reduces precision (more healthy cells removed), while being more conservative increases precision but reduces recall.
A precision-recall curve plots precision as a function of recall; usually precision will decrease as recall increases.

Examples of measures that combine precision and recall are the F-measure (the weighted harmonic mean of precision and recall) and the Matthews correlation coefficient, which is a geometric mean of the chance-corrected variants Informedness (DeltaP') and Markedness (DeltaP).

True positive rate (TPR), also called recall or sensitivity, equals TP/P (true positives divided by real positives), which equals 1 minus the false negative rate (FNR); FNR equals FN/P, which equals 1 minus TPR.

False positive rate (FPR), the Type I error rate, equals FP/N (false positives divided by real negatives), which equals 1 minus the true negative rate (TNR, specificity); TNR equals TN/N, which equals 1 minus FPR.
Positive predictive value (PPV), i.e. precision, equals TP/(TP+FP), which equals 1 minus the false discovery rate (FDR); FDR equals FP/(TP+FP), which equals 1 minus PPV.
Accuracy (ACC) equals (TP+TN)/(P+N), i.e. the sum of true positives and true negatives divided by the total population.
The F1 score equals 2 x PPV x TPR / (PPV + TPR), which is equivalent to 2TP / (2TP + FP + FN).
Balanced accuracy (BA) equals (TPR + TNR) / 2, the average of the true positive rate and true negative rate.
The phi or Matthews correlation coefficient (MCC) equals the square root of (TPR x TNR x PPV x NPV) minus the square root of (FNR x FPR x FOR x FDR).
Precision and recall can be interpreted as (estimated) conditional probabilities, where precision and recall are connected by Bayes' theorem.

subtopic: Choosing precision vs recall by cost
fact_text: It is useful to value precision over recall when the cost of a false positive is high (e.g., in medical diagnosis, a false positive can lead to unnecessary treatment and expense), and to value recall over precision when the cost of a false negative is high (e.g., in fraud detection, a missed fraudulent transaction causes significant financial loss).

subtopic: Accuracy as weighted average of sensitivity/specificity
fact_text: In machine learning terminology, sensitivity is equivalent to the recall of the positive class and specificity is equivalent to the recall of the negative class; accuracy can be expressed as the weighted average of sensitivity and specificity, weighted by the condition's prevalence.

The true positive rate (recall) depends only on positive cases and is not affected by the class ratio r, but precision has an explicit dependence on r: starting from balanced classes and gradually decreasing r, the corresponding precision decreases because the denominator increases.
A method with 90% precision and 50% recall would yield an accuracy of either 83% or 50%, depending on whether the prevalence in the dataset is 30% or 90%.
If a sample has 95 negative and 5 positive values, classifying all values as negative (100% recall and 0% precision) would give a 0.95 accuracy score.

For the example with 95 negative and 5 positive samples, classifying all as negative gives a 0.5 balanced accuracy score (the maximum bACC score is one), equivalent to the expected value of a random guess in a balanced dataset.

The predicted positive condition rate (PPCR) identifies the percentage of the total population that is flagged; for example, a search engine that returns 30 results out of 1,000,000 documents has a PPCR of 0.003%.

According to Saito and Rehmsmeier, precision-recall plots are more informative than ROC plots when evaluating binary classifiers on imbalanced data, since ROC plots may be visually deceptive about classification reliability in such scenarios.

The F-measure is a special case of the general F-beta measure for non-negative real values of beta; the F2 measure weights recall higher than precision, while the F0.5 measure puts more emphasis on precision than recall.

For classification problems with more than two classes, precision for a given class is obtained by dividing the number of true positives by the classifier's bias toward that class (how many times it predicted the class), and recall is obtained by dividing true positives by the class's prevalence (how many times the class occurs in the data); class-wise scores can be combined into an overall multi-class evaluation score such as macro F1.

In machine learning and optimal control, reinforcement learning (RL), also known as approximate dynamic programming, is concerned with how an intelligent agent should take actions in a dynamic environment in order to maximize a reward signal.
Reinforcement learning is one of the three basic machine learning paradigms, alongside supervised learning and unsupervised learning.

To learn to maximize rewards, the agent makes decisions between trying new actions to learn more about the environment (exploration) or using current knowledge to take the best action (exploitation); the search for the optimal balance between these two strategies is known as the exploration-exploitation dilemma.

In the Markov decision process framework of RL, the environment defines a transition probability (at a given time) from one state to another under a chosen action, and an immediate reward associated with that transition.

The purpose of reinforcement learning is for the agent to learn an optimal (or near-optimal) policy that maximizes the reward function or other user-provided reinforcement signal that accumulates from immediate rewards.

If the agent directly observes the current environmental state, the problem has full observability; if the agent only has access to a subset of states, or the observed states are corrupted by noise, the agent has partial observability and the problem must be formulated as a partially observable Markov decision process (POMDP).

Reinforcement learning has been applied successfully to various problems, including energy storage, robot control, photovoltaic generators, backgammon, checkers, Go (AlphaGo), and autonomous driving systems.

The trade-off between exploration and exploitation has been most thoroughly studied through the multi-armed bandit problem and, for finite state space Markov decision processes, in Burnetas and Katehakis (1997).

In epsilon-greedy exploration, epsilon is a parameter controlling exploration vs. exploitation: with probability 1-epsilon, exploitation is chosen and the agent picks the action believed to have the best long-term effect; with probability epsilon, exploration is chosen and the action is picked uniformly at random. Epsilon is usually fixed but can be adjusted on a schedule or adaptively.

The agent's action selection is modeled as a policy: a map giving the probability of taking an action when in a given state; there are also deterministic policies, which denote the specific action that should be played at a given state.

The state-value function is defined as the expected discounted return starting from a given state and successively following a policy; roughly speaking, it estimates how good it is to be in a given state.

The discounted return is defined as the sum of future discounted rewards, where the discount rate is less than 1, so that rewards in the distant future are weighted less than rewards in the immediate future.

The brute force approach to finding an optimal policy samples returns for each possible policy and chooses the one with the largest expected discounted return; this is limited because the number of policies can be large or infinite, and the variance of the returns may be large, requiring many samples to accurately estimate each policy's discounted return.

Given a state, an action, and a policy, the action-value of that pair is defined as the expected discounted return of first taking that action in that state and following the policy thereafter; the action-value function of an optimal policy is called the optimal action-value function, commonly denoted Q*.

If a policy is optimal, one acts optimally by choosing the action with the highest action-value at each state; the knowledge of the optimal action-value function alone suffices to know how to act optimally.

Assuming full knowledge of the Markov decision process, the two basic approaches to compute the optimal action-value function are value iteration and policy iteration; both algorithms compute a sequence of functions that converge to the optimal action-value function.

Monte Carlo methods are used to solve reinforcement learning problems by averaging sample returns, relying solely on actual or simulated experience rather than requiring full knowledge of the environment's dynamics.

Monte Carlo methods apply to episodic tasks, where experience is divided into episodes that eventually terminate; policy and value function updates occur only after the completion of an episode, making these methods incremental on an episode-by-episode basis rather than step-by-step.

A better solution when returns have high variance is Sutton's temporal difference (TD) methods, based on the recursive Bellman equation; TD computation can be incremental (memory changed and the transition thrown away after each transition) or batch (transitions batched and estimates computed once), with batch methods such as the least-squares temporal difference method potentially using sample information better.
Value iteration can be used as a starting point, giving rise to the Q-learning algorithm and its many variants, including Deep Q-learning methods where a neural network is used to represent Q.

Gradient-based (policy gradient) methods start with a mapping from a parameter space to the space of policies and use gradient ascent on a performance function via a noisy gradient estimate; Williams's REINFORCE method, also known as the likelihood ratio method in simulation-based optimization, is one such algorithm.

A large class of direct policy search methods avoids relying on gradient information, including simulated annealing, cross-entropy search, and evolutionary computation; many gradient-free methods can, in theory and in the limit, achieve a global optimum.

Model-based methods combine value/policy-search algorithms with a learned model of the Markov decision process's transition probabilities; for instance, the Dyna algorithm learns a model from experience and uses it to provide more modelled transitions for a value function, in addition to the real transitions.
Model-based methods can be more computationally intensive than model-free approaches, and their utility can be limited by the extent to which the Markov decision process can be learnt.

The costly exploration needed to learn an optimal policy can be reduced if some supervised data is available, for instance by learning a crude control policy and using it to initialize the Q table intelligently instead of with zeros.
TD learning has been used for modeling dopamine-based learning in the brain, where dopaminergic projections from the substantia nigra to the basal ganglia function as the prediction error.

RL research topics include actor-critic architecture, partially supervised RL, human feedback, modular and hierarchical reinforcement learning, multiagent/distributed reinforcement learning, transfer learning, intrinsic motivation, and sample-based planning such as Monte Carlo tree search.

An algorithm can be on-policy (performing policy updates using trajectories sampled via the current policy) or off-policy; the action space may be discrete (e.g. going up, left, right, down, stay) or continuous, and the state space may likewise be discrete or continuous.
Q-learning and SARSA are both discrete-action, discrete-state algorithms operating on an action-value; Q-learning is off-policy while SARSA (state-action-reward-state-action) is on-policy.
DQN (Deep Q Network) is an off-policy algorithm with a discrete action space and continuous state space, using an action-value operator.
DDPG (Deep Deterministic Policy Gradient) is an off-policy algorithm with continuous action and state spaces, using an action-value operator.

subtopic: A3C, TRPO, PPO vs TD3, SAC
fact_text: A3C (Asynchronous Advantage Actor-Critic), TRPO (Trust Region Policy Optimization), and PPO (Proximal Policy Optimization) are on-policy algorithms with continuous state spaces using an advantage operator (action-value minus state-value), while TD3 (Twin Delayed DDPG) and SAC (Soft Actor-Critic) are off-policy algorithms with continuous action and state spaces.

Deep reinforcement learning extends reinforcement learning by using a deep neural network and without explicitly designing the state space; work on learning Atari games by Google DeepMind increased attention to deep or end-to-end reinforcement learning.

Adversarial deep reinforcement learning is an active research area focusing on vulnerabilities of learned policies; studies initially showed RL policies are susceptible to imperceptible adversarial manipulations, and proposed defenses have since been shown to not fully address current vulnerabilities.

In inverse reinforcement learning (IRL), no reward function is given; instead the reward function is inferred from an observed behavior from an expert, with the idea of mimicking behavior that is often optimal or close to optimal.

Maximum entropy inverse reinforcement learning (MaxEnt IRL) estimates the parameters of a linear model of the reward function by maximizing the entropy of the probability distribution of observed trajectories, subject to constraints related to matching expected feature counts; MaxEnt IRL has been shown to be a particular case of a more general framework named random utility inverse reinforcement learning (RU-IRL).

Multi-objective reinforcement learning (MORL) is a form of reinforcement learning concerned with conflicting alternatives; it is distinct from multi-objective optimization in that it is concerned with agents acting in environments.

Safe reinforcement learning (SRL) is the process of learning policies that maximize the expectation of the return while ensuring reasonable system performance and/or respecting safety constraints during learning and/or deployment; an alternative, risk-averse reinforcement learning, optimizes a risk measure of the return such as the conditional value at risk (CVaR) instead of the expected return, which also increases robustness to model uncertainties.

Self-reinforcement learning (self-learning) does not use the concept of an immediate external reward after a transition; it only uses internal self-reinforcement provided by a mechanism of feelings and emotions, and the learning equation includes only the state evaluation, not the immediate reward.

Self-reinforcement (self-learning) was introduced in 1982 along with a neural network capable of self-reinforcement learning named Crossbar Adaptive Array (CAA), which computes, in a crossbar fashion, both decisions about actions and emotions (feelings) about consequence states.

To statistically compare RL algorithms, an agent is trained for each algorithm as closely as possible to the others; after training, the agents are run on a sample of test episodes and their episodic returns are compared using standard statistical tools for hypothesis testing, such as the T-test and permutation test.

OpenAI's Dota-playing bot utilized thousands of years of simulated gameplay to achieve human-level performance, illustrating RL's high sample inefficiency; techniques like experience replay and curriculum learning have been proposed to reduce this but add complexity and are not always sufficient for real-world applications.

RL agents trained in specific environments often struggle to generalize their learned policies to new, unseen scenarios, which is a major setback preventing application of RL to dynamic real-world environments where adaptability is crucial.

Designing appropriate reward functions is critical because poorly designed reward functions can lead to unintended behaviors, and RL systems trained on biased data may perpetuate existing biases and lead to discriminatory or unfair outcomes.

In natural language processing, RL treats text generation as a sequential decision problem, where the model's policy selects words or utterances as actions and the reward measures properties of the completed output that are difficult to express as a per-token supervised loss; early applications used policy-gradient methods such as REINFORCE to optimize sequence-level metrics including BLEU (machine translation) and ROUGE (text summarization), and to train dialogue systems.

Reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) trains a reward model on human preference judgments (annotators comparing or ranking model outputs), and the language model is then fine-tuned with a policy-gradient algorithm, commonly proximal policy optimization (PPO), to produce outputs that the reward model scores highly.
OpenAI used RLHF to train InstructGPT, released in January 2022, and ChatGPT, released in November 2022.
Direct Preference Optimization (DPO), published in 2023, fine-tunes the language model on the preference data directly, without a separate reward model or reinforcement learning loop.

OpenAI o1, released in 2024, and DeepSeek-R1, released in 2025, were trained with large-scale reinforcement learning using rewards computed automatically from the task (such as checking a mathematical answer against a reference solution or running unit tests on generated code) to produce a chain of thought before answering.

DeepSeek-R1's developers reported that reasoning behaviors such as self-verification and reflection emerged when reinforcement learning was applied directly to a pretrained base model, without a preliminary supervised fine-tuning stage.
